segments.text: Hey friends, right now I’m going to play a quiz with you.
In this quiz, I will ask you eight questions, and you have to answer
them with either “True” or “False.” Based on your answers, you will find out
whether you are more of an introvert, an extrovert,
or possibly an ambivert, which is a combination of both.
Alright, now let’s start with quiz statement No.
1: You are someone who finds attending social gatherings very draining.
Your energy decreases when you go to social events.
Even though you enjoy being there, afterward, you feel extremely exhausted.
Instead of gaining energy from meeting people, you feel drained. True
or False?
You are someone who prefers one-on-one conversations or talking in small groups
rather than interacting with large groups of people. You are the kind of person
who thinks carefully before speaking or responding to someone. Do you
prefer working alone in a quiet environment? Are you
someone who enjoys spending your free time by yourself, perhaps
with a book or engaging in a solo hobby where you prefer being alone?
Do you find loud and busy settings distracting?
And if you end up in such a situation, do you feel the need
to take frequent breaks or step away from it?
Do you prefer expressing your ideas through writing rather than discussing
them in a group, for example? Do you enjoy deep and meaningful discussions?
...compared to making small talk with a lot of people. Now, there are many more
questions, the link to which I will provide in the description. But if five
or more of your answers to these eight questions are “True,” it means
your personality leans more toward
introversion—you might be more of an introvert. On the other hand,
if you have more “False” answers, then you tend to lean more toward extroversion.
However, if you have four “True” and four “False” answers, then you might be
an ambivert—someone who enjoys solitude at times but also gains energy from social
gatherings. Now, take a look
at Carl Gustav Jung, who, in 1921, conducted a study on psychological types.
His work led to the widespread popularity of the terms “introvert” and “extrovert.”
He himself said that “There is no such thing as a pure introvert or a
pure extrovert.” This means that no person is always an introvert or always
an extrovert. If someone were completely one or the other,
they would have to be sent to an asylum or a mental institution. In reality,
we are all ambiverts to some extent. We fall into the gray areas,
where we sometimes act as introverts and at other times as extroverts.
So, Jung’s point is exactly this. Now, through this video, I don’t want
to send the message that if you are an introvert, you must remain an introvert
for life or that being an extrovert is always better. I don’t want you
to label yourself as just one thing. Instead, through this video, I want you
to understand yourself better.
I want this video to serve as a guide for you. Even if you are an introvert,
you can still achieve great things in life. Many people believe that being
an extrovert is necessary to succeed in life, but this is not
true. According to Susan Cain, the author
of the book “Quiet,” she explains in her book that...
...”The Power of Introverts in a World That Can’t Stop Talking.” If you
are genuinely an introvert, consider it a big blessing. With this nature,
you can achieve a lot in life, contrary to the common belief that you must
be extremely outspoken to succeed. So, in today’s video, I’m going to talk about
Susan Cain’s story—how she
was an introvert and how she embraced her introverted nature.
Because of this, she was treated differently, which started pushing her
life in the wrong direction. I want to tell you about the actual benefits
of being an introvert. If you are an introvert, you
should understand your strengths. I will explain what your strengths
are and how you can use them to move forward and succeed in life.
If you are an extrovert, you should also understand
the strengths of introverts, because sometimes even extroverts
need to adopt these traits—otherwise, things can go wrong. I
know this from personal experience, as I have faced such challenges myself. I
will share what went wrong for me and also tell you about five specific advantages
that introverts naturally have. These strengths are usually stronger
in introverts compared to extroverts, who might have them to a lesser extent.
Most of the time, I will explain this to you by summarizing the book “Quiet.”
I will share how, in the 19th century, the world valued and understood introverts
more. But after the 20th century, why did the focus shift more toward
extroverts? Why did society start celebrating extroverts
more? You will discover many interesting
insights about yourself and others through this discussion.
This video will help you become a better communicator, improve your people
skills, and enhance your communication abilities.
Overall, it will help you grow more in life. We will also discuss the power
of silence—what it really means and how to use it effectively. As an introvert,
if you prefer staying silent, or even as an extrovert, when
you choose to be silent, what are the advantages of it? What
is the strength of silence? This video will help you understand all of that.
So now, let’s start with Susan’s story. From childhood, Susan Cain was
an introverted person who loved reading books. Her grandfather was also
an avid reader. She remembers that whenever she visited her grandfather’s
house, it was filled with books. Whether it was the desk, chair, or any
other space, books were everywhere. And she loved that environment.
In fact, whenever her family went camping, it usually seemed like an extroverted
activity—where people are supposed to explore nature and
do outdoor activities. Her family often went camping, but instead of engaging
in typical outdoor adventures, they would sit inside the camp and read their
books. Even though they were together, they still focused on themselves.
They would sit quietly, reading books, and she loved all of this. But then, when
she went to summer camp, she had a completely opposite experience. Susan
had thought that the summer camp would be just like her family environment—where
people would wear matching outfits, read their books, and stay in their own space.
But no, it was the exact opposite experience. Because as soon as she
arrived, the camp counselor gathered everyone and announced that they would
have to cheer daily. What did they have
to cheer? “R-O-W-D-I-E, that’s the way we spell rowdy!
Rowdy, rowdy, rowdy, let’s get rowdy!” Everyone had to sing this together every
day. Now, this experience for Susan was completely different from
what she had expected.
It was nothing like she had expected. But somehow, she went along with it and
participated. After
that, she quietly returned to her camp to continue reading her book.
However, as soon as she started reading, the most popular girl in the
camp came over and gave her a disapproving look. She said, “What are you doing?
Please don’t be like this!” Because reading alone was the complete opposite
of being “rowdy.” This made Susan feel as if being alone, reading
books, and enjoying solitude weren’t cool things to do.
She was made to feel that this wasn’t something she should do. If she wanted
to be cool, she had to join in and do things with
everyone else. Now, when she had gone
to summer camp, she had packed an entire suitcase full of books—because
she wanted to spend her time reading. But since everyone around her kept saying
that being the way she was wasn’t right, she started feeling
that she shouldn’t be an introvert and instead needed to be more extroverted.
She felt that she had to join everyone, play games, be active, and behave like
others. This idea stuck in her mind. She started believing, “Maybe it’s true.
Maybe there’s something wrong with me.” So, she took her suitcase full of books,
hid it under her bed, and throughout the entire summer camp, she never took it out.
She started doing things the way others told her to. In fact, she even
chose a career based on what others wanted. She decided to focus
on becoming a lawyer. But this was the biggest problem—she never actually wanted
to be a lawyer. She was influenced by others and ended up pursuing law,
even though what she truly loved was reading and writing books.
Susan says that this happens to many people in life. There
are things we are truly interested in, but we don’t pursue
them—and because of this, we lose a lot. The world also loses a lot.
Many great things never come to life—for example, if Susan had never
become a writer, she wouldn’t have written this amazing book.
The world is wasting so many things just because it doesn’t understand that
being an introvert is not a bad thing. In her book, Susan explains
that introversion does not mean being a shy person who never talks to anyone.
No! According to her, introversion is about energy management. If you are
someone who gains energy by being alone, then it’s important to understand this.
Because many people gain energy in the exact opposite way—meaning, when they meet
others, join a group, and stay around people, they feel energized through social
stimulation. Whereas shyness is a completely different thing. Anxiety,
the pressure of social judgment—that’s another issue.
An introvert is not necessarily a shy person.
It is possible that an introvert is a very confident person, but they always
prefer being around fewer people, doing reflective work, or enjoying a
quiet environment.
And this actual personality type, which many people have—maybe
you have it too—comes with some major advantages. For example, Advantage No.
1: People who stay quiet, remain silent, and are somewhat introverted.
They have enhanced focus and a greater ability to do deep work. Their
concentration power and problem-solving ability are often higher than that
of extroverts. For example, did you know that Steve Wozniak, the co-founder
of Apple, built the first computer entirely in solitude? He was able
to dive deep into technical details and successfully create the
computer because of this.
Why? Because he was working alone in solitude. His deep understanding and
concentration allowed him to achieve many groundbreaking innovations in the
field of personal computing. Later, when he met Steve Jobs, his
work boomed significantly. If I give you an Indian example, Dr.
APJ Abdul Kalam, our former President of India, also known as the
Missile Man of India, was a soft-spoken and contemplative person.
He was an introverted type of person. It is said that many times he would spend
hours and hours in silence, deeply engaged in research. He tackled complex
scientific problems with deep work, and this was a huge advantage for him because,
in a way, his personality was also somewhat introverted. The second
advantage is thoughtful creativity. When an introvert or even a regular person
spends time in solitude and introspects, they create mental space in their mind.
A place where breakthrough ideas often emerge, imaginative work can happen, and
original perspectives can develop. For example, you must have heard
about Charles Darwin. The one who wrote about the Theory of Evolution.
He often took long walks alone. Why? So that he could organize his thoughts.
Because of those solitary walks, you could say he was able to shape the Theory
of Evolution in a very interesting way. He had a habit of observing nature
alone, and during this time,
he connected many dots and developed his theory. Another example is Dr.
Seuss, whose real name was Theodor Seuss Geisel. He often spent time
in his secluded office.
Most of his ideas and colorful rhymes came to him only when he worked in solitude,
alone in his office, without any interruptions. Did you know he was
so introverted that he even avoided meeting his young fans? Why? Because
he knew that many of these children, who loved his literature.
They loved his whimsical rhymes
and expected that he would be like Santa Claus—very outspoken,
loud, and social. But his personality was not like that at all.
He was a reserved person. Similarly, R.K.
Narayan, the renowned Indian novelist, is well known for his
gentle observational writing style. He himself has spoken about this.
They often found inspiration by spending time in a quiet environment
and a reflective space daily. This is a huge advantage of being silent and
calm, which introverts naturally possess.
Third: Listening and Empathy Introverts are usually great active listeners.
They can listen to and understand others deeply. Because of this,
they often build strong relationships and, in many cases, become effective leaders.
For example, Adam Grant conducted research on leadership, where he noticed
that introverted leaders often become more effective leaders. Why?
Because they actively listen to their team and allow
their ideas to be nurtured, compared to extroverts, who sometimes focus
more on imposing their own ideas rather than listening to others.
Now, to be honest, I am a bit of an extroverted person. So, I have
personally noticed that sometimes I tend to push my ideas onto others and talk a
lot. And when I do that, other people’s good ideas don’t always get a
chance to come out. This is a problem that introverts usually don’t have.
Introverts usually ask more questions, clarify things, and make thoughtful
decisions, which sometimes an extrovert like
me fails to do. An Indian example is Ratan Tata.
While he wasn’t overly introverted in the classic sense, he was very soft-spoken.
He had an empathetic demeanor and the ability to listen to others.
He also had a good habit of listening, and because of his approach, he was able
to build a lot of trust and loyalty within the Tata Group. This reminds me
of another point related to this, which is mentioned in the
book 48 Laws of Power: “Always speak less than necessary.”
I talked about this in one of my previous videos, where I
shared a story about a friend of mine who used to talk a lot.
He used to talk so much that no one took him seriously.
On the other hand, I had another friend who spoke very little.
But whenever he spoke, everyone listened to him seriously. Even if he wasn’t
saying anything particularly
interesting or useful, people still paid attention just because he spoke less.
That’s why people paid more attention to him. Whereas the
other friend, even when he was saying something valuable and important,
people wouldn’t pay much attention to him because he talked too much about himself.
His personality was more on the extroverted side. The next advantage
is calm, collected leadership. Many introverts, with their steadiness...
Thoughtfulness is higher in them, which helps a lot in leadership.
These people can often make balanced decisions even
under pressure and stress, and they handle situations well. If we look
at an Indian example, Gandhi Ji was very famous for his quiet strength.
His philosophy of non-violence, calm demeanor,
and reflective nature were the reasons why millions and millions of people...
...were able to understand his philosophy.
They admired his philosophy of non-violence and followed it.
At that time, without the internet, without much—you could say without
much social media—he inspired millions of people and made them his followers.
That is a big achievement. And why did this happen?
Because his nature was somewhat introverted rather than relying on fiery
speeches.
They used measured words and spoke with deep conviction. Next, another
advantage that introverts have, which extroverts often lack, is depth over
breadth. Introverts typically focus more on quality rather
than quantity—whether it’s relationships, hobbies, or expertise.
Because of this, they develop in-depth mastery over things. Extroverts,
on the other hand, often jump from one thing to another.
They keep jumping from one thing to another—sometimes inspired by one
person, sometimes by another. Even Susan talks about this.
This is a common problem seen
in extroverts. In fact, this can be observed in any large group.
Whenever we are in a big group, we usually tend to gravitate towards
the most charismatic person—the
one who is either the best-looking or the one who speaks the most confidently.
We all try to follow their ideas, even if they aren’t the best ideas for the
group as a whole. Susan has observed in several research studies that when
we are constantly surrounded by groups and act as extroverts, we struggle to bring
out our own original ideas. Instead, we keep getting inspired
by someone else’s ideas and someone else’s way of doing things.
In fact, you yourself must have noticed this when you are in a group. When
everyone is speaking in a certain way, there is a high chance
that you will also start speaking in the same way. Your way of speaking and
using language will naturally adapt. For example, many people who move
abroad or even to different states within India end up changing their accent.
Because the influence of others affects us a lot, whereas
introverts often avoid this. Do you know about J.K.
Rowling? The entire concept of Harry Potter came to her mind during a train
ride, which was also delayed. She was quietly thinking about it
on the train, and when this idea struck her, she really loved it.
She was so introverted that she didn’t even bother to ask someone for a pen
to write down her idea. If we look at an Indian example, Rabindranath Tagore,
the Indian poet and Nobel laureate, spent a significant amount of his life
in peaceful retreats. Reflecting on nature and spirituality
acted as fuel to make his poems more powerful.
His songs and philosophical works largely emerged from inner contemplation, meaning
spending time with himself. Now, look at all these advantages of being silent.
I’m not saying that if you’re an extrovert, you should become
an introvert. No, what I’m saying is that being silent is powerful. And
if you naturally know how to be silent—if you’re an introvert, which
makes up one-third
of the world’s population—then you already have a strong advantage.
One out of every three people you meet will be an introvert. If you are
one of them, then you already possess these qualities. Don’t see these
qualities as weaknesses—understand them as your strengths and
use them to your advantage. However, this doesn’t mean that you should
stay in your comfort zone and avoid doing things that you need to do.
For example, let me give Susan’s example. Susan was an introvert since
childhood. She enjoyed being alone, doing research, reading books, and writing
books—these things aligned
with her strengths, and she pursued them. However, when the need arose, she
stepped out of her comfort zone. For the promotion of her quiet book, she
went on stage and spoke publicly—embracing public speaking, even as an introvert.
She didn’t like it at all, yet she did it.
Why?
Because a mix of both (introversion and stepping out when needed) creates powerful
outcomes. Just like I gave you the example of Wozniak—when Steve Wozniak met
Steve Jobs, who was an extrovert, their combination created the best results.
That’s why a balanced approach
in life is very important. If you’re an introvert, understand your strengths.
But it’s also necessary to bring in the energy that extroverts bring to the
table. On the other hand, if you’re an extrovert, it’s important to understand
the strengths that introverts have and incorporate them into yourself as well.
You must have heard this many times—”Don’t make promises when you’re too happy, and
don’t make bad decisions when you’re too sad.” And this often happens
with extroverts. It has happened to me as well—many times when
I got too happy, I made promises to people that I later regretted.
I shouldn’t have said that, or I shouldn’t have made that promise.
On the other hand, when I got really angry or faced a problem, I made
some decisions or said things that caused issues—led to fights and pain. That’s
why I understand that the power introverts have—the ability
to think before speaking—is something I should also learn.
If you are an extrovert right now, then understand this as well.
Understanding these things will help you understand yourself better and
understand others more effectively. This, in turn, will improve
your communication skills, help you recognize your strengths, and make
you aware of your weaknesses, ultimately helping you move forward in life.
Now, Susan asks, “If being an introvert has so many advantages,
why is society so extrovert-dominated?
Why do extroverts receive so much respect?” Even though
you will find many entrepreneurs who are introverts yet extremely popular,
this phenomenon has a historical context, which is quite interesting. The author
explains that in the 19th century, there was a “Culture of Character.?
At that time, people valued modesty, integrity, and similar qualities.
A person with a strong character was respected more. For
example, Abraham Lincoln—he had a quiet demeanor, which people admired a lot.
Even the self-help books of that time focused more
on these values. But then, a cultural shift
happened—from the “Culture of Character” to the “Culture of Personality..
Earlier, the focus was more on agriculture and rural life, but then
came industrialization, urban
lifestyles, and modern education. Living in cities became more popular,
and during this time, people who were charismatic, who could speak well
in front of others, and who could lead industries started advancing more in life.
People who could manage others effectively started achieving significant
success during this time. As a result, self-help books also began to change.
Books like How to Win Friends and Influence People became more popular.
Again, this doesn’t mean that it was
wrong or bad—it was simply what people needed at that time.
There was a huge craze for becoming an extrovert. But even
today, this craze is still quite strong.
As a result, many people believe that introverts aren’t powerful enough,
can’t be great leaders, can’t study effectively, or can’t achieve success.
However, Susan says that data shows the exact opposite—that introverts actually...
Many times, they achieve better grades, score higher marks, and even become better
leaders. That’s why it’s important to understand this
in schools, colleges, and offices, where everyone is trying to turn people
into extroverts—encouraging teamwork at all
costs. Even in schools, teachers insist that children must work together.
In offices, employees are expected to collaborate all the time.
Yes, this approach is right for some time, but not always. Many people perform
better and work more efficiently in solitude, just like Susan herself.
If we want to move this world in the right direction, we need both introverts
and extroverts working together.
Only then can a team function in the best possible way.
And we can achieve even greater success. Now, Susan also gave a TED Talk related
to this topic. In this TED Talk, she shared her story
of how, when she went to camp, she took a large briefcase full of books with her.
She had hidden it away. Many people in life are just like this.
After many years, just like a suitcase, people tend to hide their personalities
and strengths inside, often because of others. But they shouldn’t hide them.
They should embrace them. They should bring them out and use them to move
forward in life. Just like Susan, who shifted her focus from becoming a lawyer
to pursuing her passion as a writer.
Because it matched her strengths and character more. Similarly, you should
also look at what’s inside your suitcase. What are your strengths?
Is it that you love reading books? Or is it that you gain energy when
working collaboratively with others? Or maybe your suitcase holds champagne?
Maybe your suitcase holds gym equipment. Whatever is in your suitcase, the main
message of this video is that you shouldn’t hide it away.
You should take it out, embrace it, and use it to move forward in life. In the
final message, Susan says—just
like she mentioned in her TED Talk—that there are three things we should do.
First, it’s not necessary to force everyone to work in groups
all the time, 24/7.
Teachers in schools and employers in offices should understand this.
Second, everyone should spend some time in the wilderness, in nature. This
doesn’t mean that you have
to quit your job and go live in the jungle or become a hermit.
That’s not necessary.
But yes, spending some time in solitude, being with nature,
can be very beneficial. And lastly, as mentioned before, take a
good look at what’s in your suitcase. Is it a trip with others?
Is it books?
Is it writing? Whatever it is, identify it. This one
thing can completely change your life.
